record transaction Notes receivable – terminology, calculate interest, record transactions ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE AND ALLOWANCE FOR DOUBTFUL ACCOUNTS Aging Analysis tells the company how much of their receivables they should expect to be uncollectable (becomes the allowance for doubtful accounts) • Can also use percentage of net sales to estimate (credit sales * estimated uncollectible) Allowance for doubtful accounts (may be uncollectible) is a contra-asset  Negative, Non-cash asset (Allowance should be subtracted from Retained Earnings to balance) Writing Off: When a receivable is officially uncollectible  Add the amount to be written off to the allowance for doubtful accounts  Subtract the amount to be written off from the receivables account  (Net 0 on the assets side, therefore it balances) CREDIT CARD RECEIVABLES The accounts receivable are due from credit company not customer, which comes with an additional fee Credit card companies deduct fee from amount they owe company Recording: ▪ Record Sale- Increase AR, Increase Revenue + NI ▪ Record Credit Payment - Increase Cash, Decrease AR, Decrease NI (Increase Credit Card Expense) NOTES RECEIVABLE Notes: Longer payment terms than accounts, charged interest (paid at maturity), company requires promissory note + collateral • Promissory Note: Legal promise to pay back sum of the note by a point in time • Collateral: Asset put up against the balance of the loan, providing security to lender Interest Calculated: Loan Amt * Annual Interest Rate * (#Months/12) or (#Days/360) Recording Transactions:  Initial Borrowing- Increase Notes Receivable, Increase Revenue/NI  Adjusting Entry- Increase interest receivable, Increase Interest income/NI  Payback – Increase Cash, Decrease Interest Receivable, Decrease Notes Receivable Chapter 6 – SE6-3 + SE6-4Chapter 6 – E6-10Chapter 6 – E6-12CHAPTER 7 Inventory concepts – companies, categories, perpetual vs periodic Cost of inventory Inventory methods – calculations and impact on gross margin, ending inventory and taxable income Lower of cost or market INVENTORY CONCEPTS Company Categories: • Manufacturer – converts raw materials and components into finished products (factory) • Wholesaler – buy finished products in large quantities, selling products to retailers in small quantities (Costco) • Retailer – buy from wholesales, resell finished products to individual consumers (Grocery Stores) Inventory Categories: • Raw Materials – Raw materials/components for production that have not been used yet • Work-in-Process – Units in production, but not yet fully assembled Finished Goods – Finished product and ready for sale Perpetual + Periodic: • Perpetual Calculation – Cost of inventory calculated after sale (continuous) • Periodic Calculation – Cost of inventory calculated after period LIFO, FIFO, WEIGHTED AVERAGE CALCULATIONS Last In, First Out: When accounting for inventory sold, you use the prices/value of the most recently purchased inventories first (Stack) First In, First Out: When accounting for inventory sold, you use the prices/value of the least recently purchased (oldest inventory) inventories first (Queue) Weighted Average Cost: Compute the average cost of a piece of inventory sold based on the entirety of the inventory before the sales were made COST OF INVENTORY Inventory Formula: Beginning Inventory + Purchase Inventory = Cost of Goods Available to be Sold. – Ending Inventory = Cost of Goods Sold • Inventory calculations directly impact Gross Margin (Sales – CoGS) • Since this directly impacts a firms Net Income, a firm benefits from selecting the highest inventory valuation to decrease its income taxes Total Inventory Formula: INVENTORY VALUATION Inventories must be reported at the lower of the cost (price paid for the inventory) or the market (market value of the inventory). Called Net Realizeable Value  If a company uses FIFO / LIFO / AC, but the market value of their remaining inventory is less than the calculated price of their inventory, the company must mark down the difference so that the ending balance of inventory reflects the lower of either the Cost or the Market  Reduces inventory, retained earnings, and net income  Increases expenses CONCEPTUAL INVENTORY QUESTIONChapter 7 – SE 7-9Chapter 7 – P 7-3CHAPTER 8 Types of long-lived assets and related expense Determine cost of long-lived asset All terms related to PPE PPE – straight-line depreciation, double declining & units of production Calculate gain/loss on sale of PPE (record transaction) Revenue expenditure vs capital expenditure When is an impairment recorded Types of intangible assets PPE ratios will be included on financial ratio handout LONG LIVES ASSETS + RELATED EXPENSETERMS RELATED TO LONG LIVED ASSETS + PPE Acquisition Costs: All costs related to the purchase of a long-lived asset (price + tax, shipping, fees, installation). Total is the asset cost. Useful Life: Period of time over which the asset is expected to generate measurable benefits Salvage Value: Amount expected for the asset when disposed at the end of its useful life • Depreciable Cost: Asset Cost – Salvage Value Depreciation method: Estimate of how the asset is used up over its useful life Accumulated Depreciation: Total Value of the portion of the asset that has been used up Book Value: Equal to Asset/Acquisition cost – Accumulated Depreciation account for that asset DEPRECIATION METHODS Straight Line: (Acquisition cost – Salvage Value)/Estimated useful life (years) Double Declining: Book value at beginning of year * Double Declining rate • Double Declining Rate: (1/estimated useful life (years)) * 2 These are both annual. Adjust accordingly for monthly! Units of Production: Depreciation per unit * Units of production for the period • Depreciation per unit = (Acquisition cost – Salvage value) / Total estimated production units CALCULATE GAIN/LOSS ON SALE OF PPE Accounts affected by selling an Asset  Remove acquisition cost (decrease asset)  Remove accumulated depreciation  Gain or loss is reported on the income statement INCOME STATEMENTCAPITAL V REVENUE EXPENDITURES Capital Expenditures: Recorded as an asset when purchased • Extend the useful life • Improve the quality • Reduce operating expense • Ex: New Heating system, replacing windows, new brakes on car Revenue Expenditures: Expenses when incurred • Ordinary maintenance and repairs • Lost-cost items • Ex: Filter change on car, maintenance on plumbing INTANGIBLE ASSETS + IMPAIRMENTS Impairments: When depreciable assets lose value, below their book value • Recorded when Future Cash Flows from an asset are less then Net Book value • Difference between the two Intangible Assets: Long term assets with no physical substance • Patents, Copyright, Franchises, Trademarks and Goodwill • Amortize over useful life, however some have indefinite useful lives CHAPTER 8 - SE 8-1 + SE 8-5CHAPTER 8 – P8-3CHAPTER 8 – SSQ- 6CHAPTER 9 Accrued liabilities, unearned revenue & accounts payable Conditions for contingent liabilities Warranties Short-term vs long-term debt Calculate interest on loan for mortgage or note Bond terms, advantages/disadvantages, and types of bonds Bond calculations - calculate bond price and straight-line amortization Bond transactions – interest expense, interest payments, proceeds, repayment Bond ratings ACCRUED LIABILITIES Expenses that have not yet been paid for or recorded in Accounts Payable Adjustments that accountants make to the balance sheet after all transactions have been entered into the accounting records, and prior to the issuance of the financial statements, so that the statements fairly present the financial condition of the company. Accruals for Routine Contractual Liabilities Include:  Wages that the company is contractually obligated to pay to employees for work performed, but not yet paid for the current period  Interest that is due in the current period on borrowed money, but has not yet been paid  Income taxes that are owed, but not yet paid, as a result of profit earned during the period  Other operating liabilities that have been incurred but not yet paid for in the current period (rent, utilities, etc.) UNEARNED REVENUE Revenue that has been received without the transfer of a good or performance of a service to the customer Cash has been received but the revenue has not yet been recorded  Advance payments for products that have not been delivered yet  Gift Cards  Companies that sell prepaid expenses (insurance, rent, Spotify year long subscriptions) CONDITIONS FOR CONTINGENT LIABILITIES Contingent liabilities depend on the occurrence of a future uncertain event in order to determine whether a liability exists, and if so, in what amount. Conditions: If the future event will probably occur and liability amount can be reasonably estimated, we record a contingent liability as an amount • If the event is probable, but cannot be estimated or possible (but not probable) it is disclosed in the financial notes • If the probability is remote, we don’t have to say anything Ex:  Litigation that has been brought against the company whose amount and outcome depend upon adjudication  Warranty liabilities for products sold which depend upon the occurrence of product defects to require the company to repair or replace the product purchased WARRANTIES Warranty liabilities are commitments that manufacturers make to their customers to repair or replace defective products within a specified period of time. Warranty expense  Increase expense and liability When the item is brought back  nothing affects income, decrease cash or inventory and liability SHORT-TERM VERSUS LONG-TERM DEBT SHORT TERM  Seasonal swings in working capital are often financed with a bank line of credit (short term debt)  Bank commits to lend up to a max. amount and the amounts borrowed must be repaid in full sometime during the year  Amount Borrowed = Note Payable (a current liability) LONG TERM  Used to fund long-term assets (like PPE);  Bonds and notes in capital markets are cost-efficient forms of LT Debt  Much more structured than short-term debt CALCULATE INTEREST ON A MORTGAGE OR NOTE Notes: Accrue interest during borrowing period, even if interest is not paid yet • ”Using” borrowings is it is an expense while “using” Mortgage: Pay off interest during annual/monthly payments • First pay off the interest portion of the loan, the rest of the payment goes towards the principal BONDS Face Amount / Principal: Amount repaid at maturity of the bond Coupon (contract / stated) Rate: The portion of the face amount that is paid as a coupon to the bondholder; Coupons are paid SEMI-ANNUALLY → divide the Coupon Rate by 2 Market (yield / effective) Rate: Interest Rate that investors expect to earn on the investment; Used to Price the Bond; AGAIN, DIVIDE BY 2 Periodic Interest Payments (SEMIANNUALLY) during the bond’s life; Called annuity because they are equal and made at regular intervals Lump Sum/Single Payment Bond: Single payment of the face value at maturity; No coupon payments BONDS -- PRICING Par Value  Coupon Rate = Market Rate  Price = Face Value Sold at a Premium  Coupon Rate > Market Rate  Price > Face Value Sold at a Discount  Coupon Rate < Market Rate  Price < Face Value BOND RATINGS Factors that impact a credit rating  Business risk: industry characteristics, competitive position, management  Financial risk: financial characteristics, financial policy, profitability, capital structure, cash flow protection, financial flexibility Ratios Moody looks at: profitability, cash flow, solvency  Highest rating: Aaa  Lowest rating: C BOND PROBLEM Premium or Discount? 1st Interest payment? 2nd interest payment? Total interest paid over the life of the bond? Present value of the bond? Total amount of amortization? FACE: 350,000 COUPON RATE: 8% MARKET RATE: 10% TERM: 9 YEARS PAYMENT: SEMI ANNUAL CHAPTER 9 – E9-14 CHAPTER 9 – P9-4 JUST DO b, c, d STOCK AND SHARES Authorized Shares: Number of shares that the Board of Directors has approved to be issued Issued Shares: Cumulative number of shares that have been sold (found on balance sheet or statement of stockholder’s equity) Outstanding Shares: Issued Stock – Repurchased Shares Treasury Stock: Repurchased Shares (negative equity acct) Par Value: is an arbitrary amount determined when the company was formed Market Capitalization: Number of outstanding shares x market price per share Book Value Per Share: Common Equity/ Average # of Common Shares Outstading PREFERRED STOCK In addition to the features of Common Stock, Preferred Stocks has …  Yield: The preferred stock is structures such that it pays regular dividends, similarly to a bond. But, dividends, unlike the interest expense on a bond, are not deductible for tax purposes  Preferred stockholders have no voting rights  Conversion privileges  Preferred stock can contain an option that allows investors to convert their preferred shares into common shares at a predetermined number of common shares per preferred share DIVIDENDS Cash Dividends  Dividends reduce Cash and Retained Earnings by the amount of the cash dividends paid Stock Dividend: shares of stock are distributed to shareholders instead of cash  Company reduced retained earnings (just as for cash dividends) and increases common stock from par and additional paid in capital accounts. Cash and the stock’s par value per share are unaffected by a stock dividend.  Amount of the dividend in dollars depends on the number of shares distributed as a proportion of the total shares outstanding Cumulative Preferred Dividends (Arrears)  Dividends on preferred stock have priority over those on common stock, including unpaid prior year’s preferred dividends when preferred stock is cumulative.  Preferred Stock typically has regular dividends; If not actually paid out in a given year, company can not pay out common stock dividends either (until the preferred stock dividends are paid)  They may be “declared” but not yet paid (because the same dividend is always paid per pref. share) CASH DIVIDENDS + STOCK TRANSACTIONS Cash Dividends • Declaration Date: Announcing Dividends to public, record liability (increase dividends payable, decrease RE) • Record Date: Must own shares by this date to receive dividend, no transaction • Payment Date: Paying dividends (decrease cash, decrease dividends payable) Stock Dividends – Distributing stock to shareholders in lieu of cash • Does not appear in any account but equity • Transaction: Increase Common Stock, Decrease RE with dividend value (dividend shares * market value), offset with Additional Paid in Capital Issuing Stock • Increase Cash, Increase Preferred/Common (#stocks * par), Balance transaction with Additional Paid in Capital (P/C) Treasury Stock – When a corporation repurchases its own stock. Negative Equity account  Repurchasing Stock: Decrease Cash, Decrease Treasury Stock  Selling Treasury Stock: Increase Cash, Increase Treasury Stock, Balance with Additional PiC Treasury STOCK SPLIT Company issues additional common shares to its existing stockholders Company desires to reduce stock price in order to improve its marketability (people are more likely to buy a less expensive stock) Stock Split has no financial statement effects!! 2-for-1 Split: If you had one share, now you’ll have 2 shares, and now they are each worth have of the value of the original one share, but together are the same as before CHAPTER 10 – SE 10-4 + SE 10-6CHAPTER 10 – E10-5CHAPTER 10 – P10-6 Stockholders Equity transactions - Can also do regular transactions (both provided in key) *Add columns for Treasury + APIC Treasury* ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE SALES ON ACCOUNT, COLLECTIONS OF ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE, ESTIMATE A LLOWANCE FOR DOUBTFUL ACCOUNTS, WRITE OFFPURCHASE INVENTORY BALANCE SHEET INCOME STATEMENT Transaction Cash Asset Noncash Asset Liabilities Contrib.
